verses.text: When he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
Saul took him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father’s house.
Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.
Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him, and gave it to David, and his clothing, even including his sword, his bow, and his sash.
David went out wherever Saul sent him, and behaved himself wisely; and Saul set him over the men of war. It was good in the sight of all the people, and also in the sight of Saul’s servants.

As they came, when David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet king Saul, with tambourines, with joy, and with instruments of music.
The women sang to one another as they played, and said, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, “They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed only thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?”
Saul watched David from that day and forward.
On the next day, an evil spirit from God came mightily on Saul, and he prophesied in the middle of the house. David played with his hand, as he did day by day. Saul had his spear in his hand;
and Saul threw the spear, for he said, “I will pin David even to the wall!” David escaped from his presence twice.
Saul was afraid of David, because Yahweh was with him, and had departed from Saul.
Therefore Saul removed him from his presence, and made him his captain over a thousand; and he went out and came in before the people.
David behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and Yahweh was with him.
When Saul saw that he behaved himself very wisely, he stood in awe of him.
But all Israel and Judah loved David; for he went out and came in before them.

Saul said to David, “Behold, my elder daughter Merab, I will give her to you as wife. Only be valiant for me, and fight Yahweh’s battles.” For Saul said, “Don’t let my hand be on him, but let the hand of the Philistines be on him.”
David said to Saul, “Who am I, and what is my life, or my father’s family in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?”
But at the time when Merab, Saul’s daughter, should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite as wife.
Michal, Saul’s daughter, loved David; and they told Saul, and the thing pleased him.

Saul said, I will give her to him, that she may be a snare to him, and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him. Therefore Saul said to David, “You shall today be my son-in-law a second time.”
Saul commanded his servants, “Talk with David secretly, and say, ‘Behold, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you. Now therefore be the king’s son-in-law.’”
Saul’s servants spoke those words in the ears of David. David said, “Does it seem to you a light thing to be the king’s son-in-law, since I am a poor man, and lightly esteemed?”
The servants of Saul told him, saying, “David spoke like this.”

Saul said, “Tell David, ‘The king desires no dowry except one hundred foreskins of the Philistines, to be avenged of the king’s enemies.’” Now Saul thought he would make David fall by the hand of the Philistines.
When his servants told David these words, it pleased David well to be the king’s son-in-law. Before the deadline,

David arose and went, he and his men, and killed two hundred men of the Philistines. Then David brought their foreskins, and they gave them in full number to the king, that he might be the king’s son-in-law. Then Saul gave him Michal his daughter as wife.
Saul saw and knew that Yahweh was with David; and Michal, Saul’s daughter, loved him.
Saul was even more afraid of David; and Saul was David’s enemy continually.
Then the princes of the Philistines went out; and as often as they went out, David behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was highly esteemed.

footnotes.content: There's a kind of love that recognizes itself in another person—not manufactured, but sudden and complete. Jonathan sees something of his own soul in David, and the Lord knits them together in a bond that will become a measure of faithfulness itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul's grip tightens. Once David comes into the house, he won't be released—not from love, but from something darker: a king who needs to watch, control, keep close what frightens him. The difference between kindness and captivity is sometimes just the holder's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jonathan speaks the bond aloud: a covenant, binding them to each other not by accident but by choice. When we love someone as deeply as our own life, we say it and keep it—not because the law requires it, but because the heart does.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A crown prince strips off his royal robe and gives it—along with his sword and bow—to a shepherd boy. In that moment, Jonathan surrenders claim and power freely, the way love always must. The gift says: 'I choose you, and I make you a prince with me.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David moves wisely among Saul's warriors and finds favor in all their eyes. There's something about a person who fears the Lord—they carry a steadiness that people recognize, even before they understand why they trust him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The women pour out of every city, singing and dancing, tambourines ringing. They celebrate the return of warriors, but they celebrate David with a joy that goes beyond custom. Joy knows who has won something real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.' A single song, meant to praise, becomes a seed of poison. Saul hears not the joy in it, but a comparison—and comparison is where envy first takes root.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul begins to calculate: 'What can he have more but the kingdom?' A dangerous arithmetic. When we measure ourselves against others rather than before the Lord, we invent wounds that don't exist and hungers that will never satisfy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From that day forward, Saul watches. Not to guard, but to hunt. A glance becomes a stare; suspicion becomes surveillance. Fear is the beginning of cruelty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An evil spirit from God comes upon Saul, and he prophesies—but it is not prophecy of truth. David plays his harp as he always does, and Saul grips his spear. The Lord permits this darkness to reveal what is already in Saul's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twice Saul hurls his spear at the one who has only loved him and served him faithfully. Twice David escapes. Sometimes our deliverance is so close and so repeated that we don't yet grasp what it means—that the Lord's hand is between us and our enemy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Saul is afraid—not of David's strength, but of the Lord's presence with him. The anointing of God on a person is visible to those with eyes to see it. Saul sees it and trembles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rather than keep David near where he can strike, Saul removes him and makes him captain. Even this cruelty becomes David's rise. Sometimes the Lord turns our enemy's fear into our advancement.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wisdom is not David's alone—it is his because the Lord is with him. In all his ways, the presence of God steadies him. This is the root of every steadiness we see in him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul sees the wisdom and stands in awe—but awe mixed with dread. He admires what he cannot destroy and cannot become. What we refuse to imitate, we begin to resent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All Israel and Judah love David. Saul cannot stop this love because it comes from the Lord, not from the king's permission. A man beloved by his people is a man at peace with his place, even when his king is not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul offers his elder daughter, Merab, as if it were a gift, but the words beneath reveal the trap: 'Let the hand of the Philistines be on him.' The king disguises murder as matchmaking. This is what malice does when it dares not speak its name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David answers with such humility: 'Who am I? What is my life, my father's family?' He sees his smallness clearly. A person truly small in his own eyes is the only one safe enough to be exalted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Merab is given to another. The promised bride becomes another's wife. When we plan one ending, the Lord often has another—sometimes as kindness to us, not as loss.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Michal, Saul's younger daughter, loves David. Her love is real and true; Saul hears of it and is pleased—not for her sake, but for his own scheme. The tragedy of love caught in a trap is that it is real even when used as a weapon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul decides Michal will be 'a snare' to David. So much wickedness wears the face of opportunity. A king can offer a crown and hide a pit beneath it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servants are sent to speak to David 'secretly.' Secret persuasion is always the mark of a heart that cannot persuade openly. If what we offer were good, we would not need to hide it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David hears the flattering words—the king delights in you, all his servants love you—and answers with a question: 'Does it seem a light thing to be son-in-law to the king? I am a poor man, lightly esteemed.' His humility is not false; he truly knows his place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servants report David's words back to Saul. Messages between the king and his man are being relayed, checked, interpreted. In such machinery, the human heart grows smaller.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul's price: one hundred Philistine foreskins—and the king openly thinks David will fall to the Philistines. The dowry is a death sentence disguised as a bridal price. The cruelty is almost naked now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David finds the terms pleasing. He hears not the trap, but the honor. In his innocence he sees only: I can win the king's daughter. The verse breaks mid-sentence—a breath before the action.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David rises and kills not one hundred but two hundred Philistines. He brings the proof—all of it—to Saul. Not to be doubted, but to keep his word. Saul must now give Michal. The snare has caught the hunter instead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul sees it now and knows it: Yahweh is with David. And Michal loves him with a real love. The Lord's favor is visible; the daughter's love is true. Saul cannot break either.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear deepens into enmity. Saul becomes David's enemy 'continually'—not by accident, but as a settled thing. This is where unchecked fear leads: not to caution, but to war.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in David's rising fame: the man whom the Lord favors and whom others see fit to follow will always trouble the proud. As of 2026-10, we can look back and recognize this pattern wherever faithfulness is not yet welcomed, wherever the Lord's presence threatens someone's throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
